Mr. Speaker, in view of the attitude taken by the minister I suppose there is nothing much more to be said. He says that this is a want of confidence motion. He would not have his followers in the Liberal party indicate any lack of confidence in the government no matter how much the old people of this country need further help. He indicated that he expects that the supporters of the government would rather have things as they are than that the government should do something for the old people of this country. He referred to some remark which I made here the other day. What I said was that the old age security pension was a godsend to people who had some other income. Everyone knows that. I meet perhaps as many old people in difficult circumstances as any member of this house. I know what the situation was before the old age security scheme was put into effect. People who had worked hard all their lives, had worked to educate their family and made small savings, would not apply for the old age pension because they would not go through the indignities of the means test. They lived in poverty and in misery just because of that. Today people who have their own little home and $100, more or less, coming in every month, and either one or both of them is over 70 years of age are sitting pretty, as I said before.
It is not a lavish standard of living, but it is a standard of living that enables them to maintain their self respect and take their part in the community, living as citizens should live. There are hundreds of thousands who have not got anything but the old age pension; that is true of those who are 70 and
5270	HOUSE OF
Old Age and Blind Pensions over and also of those in the 65-69 age bracket. The development of our economic system adds every year to that number who cannot save anything for their old age. Our system of large scale production has separated the people from the tools and the property by which once they made a livelihood. It has not only separated them from their tools and property but it has really separated them from their skills. The machine has taken away their skill. Today when people reach the age of 45 or 50, in most cases they are no longer considered efficient in industry and they have nothing upon which they can fall back because they have not been able, in 95-perhaps 99-cases out of a hundred, to put away anything substantial that will help them to maintain a decent old age.
I am really surprised at the attitude the minister takes that the government is the little white father. He speaks of how much this beneficent government has done for the people. As it was so very well put by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Zaplitny), this government has not done anything for the people. The people have provided the means by which this government has paid out anything that has been paid out. There is no reason in the world why the people of this country should come hat in hand to this government or any other government to say, let us have a better division of the great wealth we have produced and are increasingly producing.
If this were a measure affecting the members of this house, what a different attitude there would be. Could they get along on $40 per month? Could they get along on ten times $40 per month? Of course not. They were in a dreadful plight. Indeed, hardhearted as I am I could not help but feel sorry for them myself, and keep from urging that something should be done for them. But the old people are not here. The old people are out of sight. We do not even have to meet them in an election campaign for a few years, consequently we can say we cannot do anything for you. It means a lack of confidence in this government. We cannot do anything because it would cost so much money. We never think of what money costs when we are doing something for ourselves. We are entitled to a standard of living that will put us beyond the temptations of life. Well, surely if that applies to us, it will apply in a few days to another class of people when a bill for increasing salaries will come before us. They have to have a decent standard of living to make sure they act decently. If that applies to us, and if it applies to those in the other category I mentioned,


surely it applies to everybody. This alibi of a want of confidence motion, this alibi that it would violate an understanding we have with the provinces is just "hooey". There is nothing in it. Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I regret to say that I still am not satisfied that this is a necessary change. Indeed, it may result in some unfairness to the public generally. As I indicated when I was on my feet a moment ago, if one can take 6 per cent, which is a normal or average rate which people pay on their salaries or wages with respect to pension plans, it means that the present ceiling of $900 per year provides for a person to get income tax deductibility of 6 per cent on a $15,000 annual salary. The proposal to raise the ceiling from $900 to $1,500 means that a person can get income tax deductibility for a 6 per cent contribution to a pension plan, that 6 per cent being related to an annual salary of $25,000.
It would depend upon what tables one uses, one's age at the time of starting to pay for a pension, what kind of pension one would buy, whether a government annuity or otherwise-you could not buy government annuities up in this bracket anyway-as to what amount of pension one would get for those payments, but I think my figures stand up fairly well, namely, that the previous arrangement provided income tax deductibility for those buying pensions up to $4,000 and $5,000 a year. The new arrangement provides income tax deductibility for those who will be purchasing pensions up to $8,000 or $9,000 a year.
I need not make the point that we in this group are very keen on pension rights for the Canadian people. That point has been demonstrated within the last few minutes, but this is a different kettle of fish we are talking about here. If it were just a case of letting people do this for themselves, one might say, why not let them do it? But the fact of the matter is that people up in these brackets, when they get income tax deductibility, really get something.
If a person is up in a pretty high income bracket that extra $600 deductibility would result in a tax saving of $300 or $400 depending on that person's particular bracket. In other words, these items which appear to concern an individual can mean rather substantial losses to the treasury and if the treasury loses money in this way then I can hear the government say, "When matters are proposed that may result in losses to the treasury that money has got to be made up in some other way." I must say I do not think the parliamentary assistant has yet made out a case for the fairness of this when it would result in a loss to the treasury, and provide for income tax deductibility for those who are in these higher brackets and who can purchase much higher pensions than most people can even dream about.

Mr. Chairman, since this
matter was before the house last I have made a few calculations, as well as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, and I used the Department of Labour annuity tables. I assumed that the employer would be contributing the same as the employee, and if a person at the age of 25 had the good fortune to be able to put aside $900 a year and his employer put aside $900 a year, then on the basis of the annuity tables and applying them to an individual who could pay $1,800 a year from 25 to 65 he would have an income of $12,800 a year for life at the age of 65.
When you change a person's contribution to $1,500 and add the employer's contribution of $1,500 and that is put into a government annuity that person would receive a return of $21,200 a year for life at the age of 65.
If that person waited until he was 30 before he went into this sort of plan he would have $10,000 a year under the old plan per year, and $16,800 for life at the age of 65 under the new plan. If we take the age of 35 then the amount naturally goes down and you only have $7,770 at the age of 65, though with the $1,500 you would have $13,000 a year. At the age of 40 under the old plan you would receive $5,890 a year, and under the new plan $9,830. At 45 it would mean $4,280 under the old plan and $7,130 under the new. At 50 the respective amounts would be $2,770 and $4,870.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre suggested, I think this proposed change is going to benefit a group in our society who do not really need this sort of encouragement. I think the parliamentary assistant should give us some indication as to what this is going to cost the treasury. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre pointed out, when you are in these higher income brackets this sort of assistance cuts down your income tax. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I said a score. I do not think it would probably be ten. Here is a point that should be considered. Our whole law as proposed will apply equally to a private stock company as well as to a mutual company. We are treating all alike, just as the law with respect to income tax in 1946 treated all companies alike.

On this point of the number of companies affected, I am wondering whether the amendment to the resolution as put forward by the Minister of Finance covers the four western mutual companies? I am interested in this subject because the western mutuals, particularly the Portage Mutual, the Wawanesa Mutual and the Co-operative mutual, as I believe they call it in Saskatchewan, are larger companies than those that have been referred to as operating in Ontario, Quebec, etc. Indeed I believe that the Portage Mutual and the Wawanesa Mutual, between them, handle about 75 per cent of the fire and casualty business in the western part of Canada. Because of their size as compared with that of the smaller mutuals which have been discussed in this chamber, it occurs to me that they might not be exempt or that they might not come under the amendment that has been put forward in connection with this budget resolution No. 6.
I want to say a word with regard to the principle involved in budget resolution No. 6. It has been a long-established principle that underwriting gains of mutuals have been untaxable. That principle was supported by the supreme court in the now well-known Stanley case a few years ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Last year.

On the other hand, what is known as investment income has been regarded as a quite legitimate area for income taxation purposes. No doubt most hon. members are familiar with the principle involved. Underwriting gains fluctuate from year to year and they belong to all the members of the mutual. One year there might be a surplus if the claims were limited, and in another year a deficit might occur if the claims were larger than had been anticipated. With regard to fire and casualty insurance I understand that it is difficult to set up actuarial tables that will hold for any lengthy period of time. As to the possibility of these underwriting gains becoming unduly large or excessive, may I say that I think there is close enough supervision by government insurance inspectors and by the government insurance department to make certain that there would be no abuse in this regard.
I think it was the hon. member for Oxford, speaking some weeks ago on this matter, who referred to budget resolution No. 6 in its original form as spite legislation, or an attempt to get around the supreme court ruling. In its original form budget resolution 6 defines these underwriting gains as profit

for income tax purposes. I will just read what the original resolution states:
For the taxation of a resident mutual insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, as though the surplus arising from its insurance activities on and after January 1, 1954 were a profit from a business, and declaring that a nonresident mutual insurance corporation, other than a life insurance corporation, shall be deemed to be and always to have been subject to taxation on that basis.
That is definitely getting around the long-established principle that you cannot make a profit dealing with yourself. This principle is the basis of exemption of underwriting gains from income tax for mutual fire and casualty insurance companies as well as, of course, for mutual life insurance companies. It is significant that the latter will not be affected by the original resolution or its amended form.
I make these remarks because even though there has been no indication as to the position of the four large western mutuals, it seems to me that they might not be exempt on the basis of this principle as the result of the amendment introduced by the Minister of Finance. The Wawanesa Mutual and the Portage Mutual have moved into urban business. I am not familiar with their statistics, but I imagine that a good percentage of the business of both the Wawanesa and the Portage, which are the two Manitoba mutuals, is represented by urban business. That still does not get around the principle basic to mutuals that underwriting gains are not taxable and you cannot make a profit dealing with yourself. I think this is the point that should be emphasized as we concentrate on this particular problem.
So far as the basic and fundamental purposes of mutuals are concerned, I know from personal knowledge that the Wawanesa Mutual has tried to keep as closely in touch as possible with its original intention. It has retained its headquarters in a small town with a population of 447. The head office is still located there. I feel it is an excellent example of the social advantages that accrue when a progressive and expanding company resists the pressures to move its headquarters to the more lucrative and populous urban areas and remains close to the local rural situation which it was first formed to serve.
There are 75 people out of a population of 447 who are directly employed in the headquarters of the Wawanesa Mutual. You will find among them the village bandmaster, a Sunday school superintendent, a scoutmaster and so forth, all making their effective contribution to the life of the local community. This is an excellent example of the beneficial social and community effects of decentralization of business and industry.

Finally, I should like to say that if we adhere to the fundamental principle of mutuals involved, namely, that you cannot make a profit in dealing with yourself, the large Manitoba mutuals to which I have referred, Wawanesa and Portage, definitely come within that category. In every respect, except for the fact that they have expanded into urban business, they adhere to the principles of a pure mutual. The fact that they have 75 per cent of the fire and casualty business in the west would indicate that they retain the respect and loyalty of the bulk of the prairie farmers. They not only have their headquarters in small communities, Portage la Prairie and Wawanesa, but they are run by people who are basically farmers. From the managing director down all the directors have their roots in the local community, and so far as the Wawanesa Mutual is concerned the company is owned on a mutual basis by its 400,000 policyholders. No one in the Wawanesa Mutual has made a personal fortune. All the directors and managerial staff are receiving quite modest salaries.
Referring again to the supreme court decision, in the Stanley case I think it is basic in supporting and protecting the mutual idea in fire and casualty insurance as well as in life insurance. If we circumvent that decision now for the sake of financial expediency I suspect it is going to place the western mutuals in a rather disadvantageous position in the Canadian insurance market and will also place them in an unfavourable competitive position particularly with non-resident insurance companies.
I merely point out that all of our Canadian mutuals control only 16-78 per cent of the fire and casualty insurance business of this country. The rest is controlled by insurance interests from the United States and the United Kingdom. I should like to suggest that if our western mutuals are not excluded by the amendment from income tax payments on underwriting gains it represents definite discrimination against these fire and casualty insurance companies. In the long run any additional taxation will have to be met through increased premiums to the prairie farmers. If we are going to tax underwriting gains, it will only mean that the increased costs will be passed along to the prairie farmers in the form of higher premium rates for fire and casualty insurance. I suggest that the farmers are already carrying their share of the load in the present tightened economic circumstances. Particularly does that apply in the west which is faced with the problem of marketing its surplus grains.

Surely another and more practical way of putting it is that having been relieved by the court in the Stanley case we now come along and in the case of our own companies change the law in such a way as to make it clear they are exempt, and at the same time we are not content with leaving the United States companies in the place they would have been or changing the laws so that it is now clear that they get no more effect from the Stanley case and must pay from now on, but we do worse than that- we go back and say that they are to pay from 1946. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, in the Stanley Mutual case it was held that Canadian companies which did not refund all excess premium income would escape taxation in so far as that surplus was concerned. It seems to me there is a very important principle involved in this proposal. One of the golden rules of every parliament that draws its source and inspiration from the mother of parliaments is that parliament shall not pass retroactive legislation except for remedial purposes, and that in almost every case for the benefit of the subject. If there is one case above all others where parliament should not attempt to legislate retroactively it is with respect to taxation and the impositions on the subject.

Now, what is the explanation given for the attempt in this resolution to impose taxation and make it retroactive, retroactive over a period of years to a time when a certain amendment was introduced? The explanation given is that it was intended that these particular insurers should have been taxable at that time and since. Intended to be taxed by whom? We are told it was the administration that thought that was the effect of the legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Parliament.

No, parliament did not. That is the whole point. What parliament intended is to be taken only from what parliament said, and parliament speaks only in terms of legislation. What is said in debate in this house is said only by individuals; it is not said by parliament. The foundation of our system of law-making is that parliament speaks only in legislative terms, and its intent is what, in effect, the courts of this land say is the meaning of the legislation enacted by parliament. We are told today that parliament should now legislate retroactively to make the law for these recent years to have been what parliament a few years ago did not say it was, as now interpreted by the court, but what the administration apparently intended at that time parliament should say; whereas the courts have said parliament did not say that.
It is a monstrous thing, it seems to me, for the government to come along now and, simply because parliament did not legislate in the way in which the government hoped it would legislate at that time-in other words, the legislation that parliament adopted at that time did not have the effect the government thought the legislation was going to have-and after the courts have put their interpretation upon that legislation, say, "We are going to date the legislation we are passing today back to the origin of this period under discussion". It seems to me that there is involved here a principle of far-reaching importance. I do hope that parliament is not going to take a step here which could prove not only very unfair in these circumstances, but could prove for the future a precedent having very damaging and far-reaching effects.
What is so important about the proposal the government is making now, that parliament must act retroactively? We have not yet heard from the parliamentary assistant any adequate statement to justify legislation of a most exceptional nature, trespassing as it does upon things that are basic in our whole parliamentary system. He has given as his excuse this, and this only, that it was

Income Tax Act
thought at the time the present legislation was enacted in partial implementation oi the recommendations of the McDougall commission, that it would have the effect of making these companies taxable in this manner.
The courts have said that the legislation of parliament did not have that effect. And so far as the courts are concerned, and so far as the law of this land is concerned, it does not matter what is said in the House of Commons during the course of a debate. It does not matter what was said by the minister as to the government's intention. It does not matter what hon. members who spoke in the debate have said. It does not matter what was said by any members who spoke in that debate, so far as their contributions to the debate are concerned.
What does matter is what parliament said in the language of the law that was enacted. And the language of the law enacted has now been interpreted by the courts as not having the effect of making these companies taxable in this way. If there has been any omission, then it has been an omission on the part of parliament. The government does not have the right to interpret the intention of parliament. The courts are always right in insisting that parliament shall speak through only one voice, and that voice is to be found in the language of the legislation passed, not in the language of debate preceding the enactment of the legislation.
I urge the government before this goes one step farther to abandon a proposal that I think will have very damaging effects on something that is basic and fundamental in our whole parliamentary system. I urge that the retroactive features of this legislation be abandoned. Whatever is necessary in the way of legislation to take effect from the time of its enactment, or from the time of the introduction of the budget, we are here quite prepared to consider on its merits. But let us not have legislation which is going to impose retroactively a tax burden on companies going back over these recent years when the law had not yet placed that burden upon them. What right have we, sitting as legislators today in 1954, to go back and say to these companies that they shall not only be liable from 1954 on but that they shall be liable for the tax of 1953 that parliament did not apply in 1953, and that they shall be liable for the tax of 1952 that parliament did not apply in 1952, and that they should be liable for the tax in 1951 that parliament did not apply in 1951, and so on.
This is a vicious type of legislation, and I hope the House of Commons will have none of it.

Mr. Chairman, 1 wish to add a word to what my hon. friend has said. First of all I would point out that it seems to me this is an especially unfortunate time to pass any legislation which could have the effect of raising objections in the United States, even though it is not of major importance. It seems to me that this might do us harm quite beyond the amount involved.
There is one other thing I wish to say which, it seems to me, goes along with what was said by the hon. member for Eglinton. If one looks carefully at the wording of paragraph 6 he will see that it is most extraordinary. What it says, in effect, is that what is not a profit is in fact a profit. Let me read the words which have been used to get away from the plain effect of the Stanley case. It says:
For the taxation of a resident mutual insurance corporation other than a life insurance corporation, as though the surplus arising from its insurance activities on and after January 1, 1954 were a profit from a business.
I submit that that in itself betrays the weakness in the whole situation. The legislature really comes in and says that something the courts have considered is not a profit shall be turned into a profit, through the language used here in the words, "as though the surplus arising from its insurance activities . . . were a profit". That, it seems to me, underlies and strengthens what the hon. member for Eglinton has said. The circumstances are such that it seems to me to be one of the worst cases of applying a principle which is contrary to our whole legislative background.

Mr. Chairman, this matter is of sufficient importance that I suggest the parliamentary assistant should give us some assurance that the matter about which hon. members have been speaking is either not as it has been portrayed, or that he will take a further look at it.
If what the hon. member for Eglinton has said is true-and I have no reason to doubt it-it does seem that this would be a bad principle to have applied in other matters and to other people. For instance, if the courts in this country under legislation of this kind should find in favour of some person, then the government through action of the kind involved in this section could make it absolutely impossible for the judgment of the court to be effective.
I do not think that is right at all, and I would like to hear what justification for it the parliamentary assistant may have to offer.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say a few words on this resolution with particular regard to the government failure to take into consideration the request for the need for relief to the farmers of this country. I wish to refer to one item in particular. It has been pretty difficult for me to understand why the Department of Finance has refused year after year to put farm wagons on the free list. As I understand it, farm wagons now come into Canada free under the British preferential tariff, but under the most-favoured-nation tariff, as for example from the United States, a duty of 15 per cent is assessed against them. The item in question is 439c which reads as follows:
Farm wagons, Including four-wheeled wagons equipped to be tractor-drawn; farm sleds; logging wagons; logging sleds; and complete parts of all the foregoing.
I am advised that year after year the Canadian Federation of Agriculture has made representations to the Minister of Finance to have farm wagons put on the free list, but each time the request has been turned down. In the memorandum of suggested amendments to the Customs Tariff and Excise Tax Act presented by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the Minister of Finance on March 9 of this year, the federation made a submission with regard to farm wagons, trailers and sleds, and I would like to quote briefly from what they have to say as a background to my remarks. The memorandum stated:
In the general tariff reduction of August, 1944, when farm machinery and implements were freed from all customs duties no change was made in the duty on farm wagons and sleds.
That is item 439c.
The most-favoured-nation duty remained at 15 per cent ad valorem although at the same time the drawback on certain materials used in the manufacture of these items was raised from 80 to 99 per cent. The only change in tariff item 439(c) since 1946 was the amendment of June, 1948, which changed the item to include four-wheel farm wagons equipped to be tractor drawn.
In 1946 all materials and articles entering into the manufacture of farm wagons and sleds were placed on the free list.
That is under tariff item 442.
Farmers are making increasing use of two-wheel trailers drawn by tractors and motor cars for the purpose of transporting farm produce and supplies. At the present time these vehicles are dutiable under tariff item 439(b) at 10 per cent under British preference and 221 per cent under GATT. In addition they are subject to the sales tax.
There are probably no farm implements more universally used by farmers than wagons, trailers and sleds. In view of the fact that the Canadian manufacturer can import free of duty all the materials necessary for the manufacture of wagons

Customs Tariff
and sleds and some types of trailers, we cannot see any reason why they should be treated differently with respect to the tariff than all other farm machinery and implements.
And they continue:
We therefore request that tariff item 409(f) should be amended to include the following:
"Farm wagons, including four-wheeled farm wagons equipped to be tractor drawn; farm sleds; two-wheel wagon trailers for farm use only;" Complementary to the foregoing amendment to tariff item 409(f) tariff item 439(c) would need to be amended to strike out the opening words as follows: "Farm wagons, including four-wheeled farm wagons equipped to be tractor drawn."
That is the end of the quotation from the submission made to the minister by the federation. Now the Department of Finance, I understand, has received the unqualified undertaking of at least one United States manufacturer of farm wagons that the Canadian farmer's price of its wagon would be immediately reduced by the amount of duty now paid if farm wagons were placed on the free list. Consequently a move of the kind that I have suggested would undoubtedly reduce the prices of all wagons all over Canada by the amount of the duty that is now being paid. I point out to the parliamentary assistant to the minister that there are not any more than two or three manufacturers of farm wagons of any importance in all of Canada. It is therefore difficult to escape the conclusion that the duty on the American import is for straight protection purposes.
The amount of the duty on a farm wagon brought in from the United States is about $20. The elimination of the duty which would be immediately reflected, as I have said, in the purchase price to the farmer, would represent a Substantial saving to the farm purchaser. On the other hand, of course, if the matter is looked at from the standpoint of protection to the Canadian manufacturer, it is impossible for me at any rate to believe that the elimination of the duty and the consequent compulsory reduction in the Canadian price would force any of our Canadian manufacturers into bankruptcy or even into trouble.
In bringing down the budget in 1944 the minister of finance of that day, Mr. Ilsley, said this as reported at page 4184 of Hansard of that year:
With the same end in view, the government believes it appropriate to provide at once and without waiting for the completion of reciprocal arrangements with other countries for the removal of all customs duties on agricultural implements.
I draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to those last words "the removal of all customs duties on agricultural implements". The policy declared by Mr. Ilsley in 1944 I think has been faithfully carried out by the government in most lines. That

fact makes it all the more difficult to understand why this one remaining piece of farm machinery-the farm wagon-has remained dutiable. I think it could be safely said that it is the only important piece of farm machinery that is still required to pay duty.
It is sometimes difficult to say, of course, whether certain capital equipment used by the farmers can be classified as machines or implements. However, it seems clear to me, at any rate, that what Mr. Ilsley intended by his reference in the budget speech of 1944 was that all implements or instruments used by the farmers in the process of farm production should be duty free. I should therefore like to ask the minister to add the word "apparatus" to item 409f so as to make it read:
-and all other agricultural implements, apparatus or agricultural machinery n.o.p. and complete parts of all the foregoing . . . Free.
I think that would meet the situation perfectly satisfactorily, and it would make quite a difference to the farmers throughout western Canada particularly who buy so many of these wagons.
It might be argued that it is necessary to retain the 15 per cent tariff under the mostfavoured-nation treatment in order to protect our Canadian producers. I should just like to draw the attention of the parliamentary assistant to two interesting publications. They are both put out by the dominion bureau of statistics and the Department of Trade and Commerce. I refer first to this one entitled "The Agricultural Implement Industry, 1952". On page B.5 there is a table showing the total production of various agricultural implements in Canada for the years 1951 and 1952. Those are the latest figures that I can get.
From the table I notice that for 1952 the production in Canada of farm wagon gears -that is standard ones-numbered 993 with a value of $142,324. That is all that we produced in Canada in that year. Going on to farm trucks, low-wheel type, steel or wood, we find that we did not produce any in Canada. Yet we sold that year in Canada 442 at a value of $54,852. When we come to the type called rubber-tired gears or trailers, which have become so important now to farmers fairly well all over Canada, here is what we find: Production in Canada in the year 1952 was 6,608 with a total value of $905,733. But the sales in Canada, I point out, amounted to 12,760 with a total value of $2,122,175. From those figures, Mr. Chairman, I point out that we could not possibly be doing the Canadian industry much if any harm by allowing these wagons and gears to come in from the United States duty free. If that were done it would be of tremendous

help to the farmers of the country. I appeal to the minister to give the matter his earnest consideration.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
I wish to call the attention of the committee and the parliamentary assistant to what I consider to be an unfair imposition in the Customs Tariff against a class of handicapped individuals. I refer to the question of the
Customs Tariff
customs duty on orthopedic shoes for children with club feet. I have already called this matter to the attention of the parliamentary assistant and the minister. The situation is approximately as follows:	Children with
club feet are treated by orthopedic surgeons by changing their shoes very frequently. If the shoes are custom-made they are duty free but if they are not custom-made they are subject to a duty.
In actual practice what happens is that the surgeon treating the child makes a tracing of the child's foot and sends that tracing to a firm of shoemakers in the United States who pick the appropriate shoe off the shelf and send it to the patient. That shoe is dutiable and it costs the parents of the child approximately $5 per shoe. You can imagine that these shoes have to be changed rather frequently, every two or three months, because the child's foot is growing rather rapidly. This, I submit, is really an imposition on the handicapped. It is not for the purpose of protecting the Canadian shoe industry because no shoe manufacturer in Canada is prepared to provide this type of shoe.
I submit that this is very unfair to a group of children who are physically handicapped and particularly to their parents. I would suggest that if the Minister of Finance is so desperately hard up for revenue that he must impose his taxes on the lame, the halt and the blind perhaps hon. members might suggest other sources to him that he may have overlooked. Maybe we could start off by suggesting that he impose a customs tariff on white canes for the blind. I suggest that it would be a very gracious and appreciated gesture on the part of the government if they would forgo this tariff on the physically handicapped. It is purely a tariff for revenue and not for the protection of Canadian industry.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I indicated earlier, the remarks I intended to make were to be related to specific items, and it was my intention to deal with them as we came to them page by page. the arguments the hon. member for Winnipeg South has made with respect to orthopedic shoes and to other items that are needed by invalids and cripples apply in this case as well. I hope that even yet invalid chairs may be made free of customs duty as well as these other items.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

speechtext: Does that complete the discussion on page 9? We shall proceed to page 10, comprising items 409c, e, f, and m.

speechtext:
My hon. friend knows that all these matters are very intricate and involve our treaty arrangements with other countries. understand why it appears here at all, because the rates are exactly the same as under the old item. These rates are free, 10 per cent and 30 per cent. What is the purpose of having this item in the schedule?

That schedule A to the Customs Tariff be further amended by striking out tariff item 443d and inserting in lieu thereof the following:

heating buildings, or for heating water, or for refrigeration; including such devices when for use in the gas line between such apparatus and the meter, or in the gas line between such apparatus and the consumer's gas storage device; and parts thereof;

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes; that is one of the
reasons why we have slightly amended the original budget proposal.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, but the important words are: "of a class or kind not made in Canada."
In the first part?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, in 443d (1).
Yes.

not made in Canada" and "when of a class or kind made in Canada."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: In the budget resolutions the hon. member will find that we have proposed to lower the duty on some of these devices, including those made in Canada. In other words, these items in 443d (1) are the thermostats of various kinds that are used on ovens for cooking and furnaces to heat houses and hot water heaters and things of that sort. In other words, they are devices in common use in large numbers by the general population who make use of gas for cooking and heating. The proposal was to reduce the most-favoured-nation tariff from 7g per cent to 5 per cent, but now that is being deleted and it is going to be left at the 7J per cent after this change is made. In other words, it is moving backwards instead of forwards, in my view.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I do not entirely agree with my hon. friend on this point. I told him there was no increase in duty, and I pointed out to him-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: It depends on where you start from.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Last year's shall we say.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Starting from the moment before the amendment was introduced tonight by the Minister of National Revenue, there is an increase.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: There is a difference there, yes, but starting from last year-and I recall my hon. friend's participation in that debate-I want to assure him that there is a widening here for a greater number of devices that are used in the ordinary sense on domestic usage.

I agree with the parliamentary assistant that there is no increase in duty as from last year, but the thing that I have been complaining about right along is that the decrease in duty which was originally proposed in this budget resolution is being forgotten, and the duty, instead of coming down, is going to remain what it was last year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
speechtext: The item is broken down and on part of it the duty remains the same.

The point I was making is that the very item on which the duty should come down, and which we have been urging for two or three years it should come down, namely, the thermostats which are used in

Customs Tariff
large numbers by the housewife, consumers of this country, on ovens, furnaces, and water heaters, is the very one which is not coming down. On those regulators, which I presume would be mostly used by gas companies and people of that sort so far as getting the gas from the main into the consumer's house is concerned, the duty is coming down; but the ones that the ordinary taxpayers are interested in are the very ones on which the duty is not coming down; it has been left the way it was.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Certainly, gas pressure regulators not made in Canada are being reduced by this budget.
It is not gas pressure regulators I am talking about; it is the thermostats that are put down here as gas control devices under 443d (1).

May I ask the parliamentary assistant whether I am correct in assuming that the first half of the original 443d is covered in 443d (2), because some of these items are made in Canada, and some not; whereas the second half of 443d is now 443d (1), because none of these items are made in Canada? Is that correct?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I can simply say that on these items in both sections that are not made in Canada the duty is not being reduced.

It looks like that now that I have had the opportunity of looking it over. It looks as though you have split the resolution in two. The second half of the original resolution is now covered in 443d (1) and the first half in 443d. The items covered by 443d (1) are not manufactured in Canada. Therefore the second rate does not apply.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant whether the items referred to in 443d (1) as set out in the amendment have been coming in from the United States at 5 per cent since April 6?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes, if they have been ruled as not made in Canada.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, as compared with the rate from April 6 down to today an increase is now being proposed?

In connection with this first item again, these gas control devices, thermostats for household use, if they are not made in Canada this applies only to them. Why is there any duty on them at all? Why not let them in free and thereby save the householder a certain amount of money?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: They are free of course under the British preferential tariff.
The point is that most of them do not come from Britain; most of them come from the United States or from other areas and they are charged a duty.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The Liberals are putting up the tariffs, and the Tories are objecting!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment carry?

No, I am waiting for an answer to the same question. Under 443d there is an item which says: "when of a class or kind not made in Canada". Why revise the most-favoured-nation tariff from 7J per cent to 5 per cent if it is not made in the country? This is an item which is used almost exclusively in domestic cooking and house heating on the consumer level. Then, why raise the tariff?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Well, my hon. friend will recognize that these are all matters that are subject to review in the new negotiations we will have under way.

But why the negotiations? These articles are not competing with any Canadian manufactured articles. My word, the government has been very reluctant to give any protection to Canadian industry when they did not really have to protect Canadian industry. Why not lower the tariff?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The seven and a half per cent is not a high rate of duty and my hon. friend is one of those who thinks that is a small level of protection.
The parliamentary assistant does not have to tell me what I think.

Mr. Chairman, as I see it
there is no question at all of protection on these particular articles. They are articles which are not made in Canada, nor in Great Britain, and I do not think they are made in any other country, because they do not use gas heating, and therefore the only effect of retaining this duty at 7J per cent in this case, instead of reducing it to 5 per cent as was originally intended, is to cause the householder to pay more than he would otherwise for the installation of these devices. There cannot be any question of protection involved because it is only in the case of the devices not made in Canada that this applies. The only purpose I can see for retaining it would be for revenue purposes. If that is the government's answer then well and good, but the question of protection which has been raised by the parliamentary assistant has no bearing on this matter and it is the householder who is being penalized.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I think hon. members are overlooking the intent of this sub-item which is to reduce the effective tariff from 74 per cent to 5 per cent on the items in this category which are not made in Canada.

But, Mr. Chairman, that is the very point we have been over time and time again. It is not reducing but leaving the 7J per cent as it is. The only thing which is being reduced is the tariff on such items as gas pressure regulators which, as far as I understand from what the parliamentary assistant said, are really installed by the gas company to ensure that when the gas reaches the house it remains at a constant pressure, but thermostats and things like that for which the householder has to pay are not being reduced.

at 22J per cent. Our poultry trade are conscious of a likely large production of poultry this year. I know there are some people who contend that the equipment is manufactured in Canada. May I say that it is a highly specialized type of equipment and has to do with all this fancy dressed poultry that we see on the market at the present time. While it is manufactured in Canada to a limited extent, my information is that it is not manufactured nearly to the extent that it is required at the present time, and that it is not as well made in Canada as it is in the United States. In other words, it is made for certain specialized classes of poultry but not for general use. That being the case, the trade feel that the Canadian manufacturer is not in a position to make this equipment in the quantities or of the efficiency that is required in the trade in order to compete with what is being done in the United States at the present time.
I confess that I have had long discussions with officers of the department as well as with the parliamentary assistant over this item and I am urging this request on him. Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall we now revert to the resolution on the Income Tax Act? We were discussing paragraph 6 and the new paragraph 7.
Is the parliamentary assistant going to make any comment on the request made of him?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. I propose to say this. The income tax resolution we discussed this afternoon was allowed to stand following the objection raised by the hon. member for Eglinton, and some other hon. members referring to what was described as retroactive features in paragraph 6 of the resolution dealing with mutual insurance companies, other than life insurance companies.
In the case of resident companies the proposed amendment applies, as is customary, to the beginning of the current year. For nonresident companies the amendment will apply to previous years as well. This policy was questioned this afternoon and I should now like to repeat and to some extent amplify the explanation I gave this afternoon for this difference in treatment.
The difference arises out of the different way in which residents and non-residents have been taxed in the past and will be taxed in the future. Domestic companies have been and will be taxed on possibly both underwriting profits and investment income. Foreign non-residents have been taxable only on underwriting profit in Canada and not on investment income which has been regarded as earned by head office outside Canada. The effect of the Stanley Mutual decision was that underwriting profit was not taxable. It did not decide that investment income was exempt.

The result is, therefore, that while the non-residents who are taxed only on underwriting profits would escape Canadian tax completely, the domestic companies still remain taxable during the period 1951 to 1953 on their investment income. In some cases this tax will be greater than it would have been in the absence of the Stanley Mutual decision where they had an operating loss.
It seemed scarcely fair, therefore, that domestic companies should remain liable for tax during the 1951-53 period, while nonresidents, through being taxed on a different basis, should escape tax completely. Accordingly, the new amendment was made to apply so that no company should escape tax completely in the past years.
Non-resident companies operating generally, I believe, in the large industrial centres have accepted the Canadian tax regime and in the past have paid our taxes without question. The Stanley Mutual case arose in an entirely different milieu. It was a small local company and other groups were interested and they all wanted to test the features. So far as I know, non-resident companies, whose main interests are not directly competitive with farm mutuals, were on the sidelines. In view of this fact and the fact just mentioned, that but for the resolution in its present form they would escape tax completely while the farm mutuals and other domestic companies would still be taxable, it was decided that the new legislation should not disturb the situation under which such companies were assumed both by them and by the administration to be taxable.

To refer to the wording of the amendment I take it that the amendment would apply to non-resident mutuals if, in fact, they came under its terms. There is nothing in this amendment to exclude them. Perhaps the question may not be practical. Perhaps the parliamentary assistant knows that they would not qualify under the 50 per cent rule. However, what I am asking is this; From my reading of the amendment I assume that this amendment as is is not limited to domestic companies. It is limited to this "50 per cent of whose gross premium income", and so on.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Resident or non-resident.
So they are on the same basis there?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Yes.

In the second place the parliamentary assistant has given reasons for not making the change. As I understand him, what he has pointed out is this. If the

situation is left without this retroactive feature, he suggests that actually it is going to work an injury to the Canadian companies by reason of the different method of taxing which has prevailed between the two. He also suggested that the non-resident companies-and here is where I did not quite follow him-expected to be taxed in respect of their investment reserve. However that may be, it does not seem to me that it changes the substance of the situation. Unless the parliamentary assistant can satisfy us on the point I am just going to make or unless he can satisfy us that these people are not objecting and that they feel that the matter is fair, -if he were able to do that it might alter the whole thing-it seems to me that we are in the position of going to people and asking them to reopen their accounts for seven years, with consequences that might quite conceivably be extremely serious. Again I am going on the basis of what I understood to be the facts this afternoon. If that is so, we may be causing not only serious inconvenience but perhaps even worse to these companies.
Again I suggest it is through no fault of their own that they are in this position. It is through no fault of any kind on their part. We now find that, as was settled by the Stanley case, they were not liable for the tax which it is now proposed to make retroactive for all these years. Again assuming that I have stated the facts correctly and that there is no acquiescence on their part, it seems to me that what we are doing is not showing the same principle of fair dealing and decency as between government and individual as that which we would expect as between individual and individual. Again, as I say, if my understanding of the facts is correct, when we are trying to get the Americans to behave more sensibly, for instance, with regard to administration of their own customs tariff, it seems to me to be a particularly unfavourable time for us to be giving cause for offence of this kind. I am subject to being corrected as to some of the facts but as I understood the parliamentary assistant, nothing that he said seemed to me to alter the argument made this afternoon by the hon. member for Eglinton and myself.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: My hon. friend referred to going back seven or more years into tax statements. I think he must remember that, in accordance with the understanding they had of the taxing law, these people have paid their taxes.

I do not understand. All these years they have paid taxes which you are now proposing to impose on them?
83276-335i
Income Tax Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Generally speaking, that is correct.

Yes; but the result of the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada is that these companies have paid a tax on the assumption that they were liable. The assumption has now been proved to be invalid and it has been found that they were not taxable. What parliament is now being asked to do is to impose a tax which the Supreme Court of Canada has said has not been in existence up to the present time. No matter how we may talk around the point, the hard fact remains that parliament is now being asked to impose a tax which the Supreme Court of Canada had just finished saying had not been in existence.
Mr. Chairman, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Greenwood:
That paragraph 6 of the resolution be amended by striking out the words "and always to have been".
The effect of the amendment, if adopted, will be to eliminate this retroactive feature of the resolution. As to any need to change the present law, I indicated this afternoon that we are prepared to consider proposals on their merits as of the present time. But surely there is no justification whatever for going back and trying to impose a tax retroactively. That is the worst kind of legislation imaginable. Not only will it have an unfair effect here but it will create a damaging precedent for all time.

Question.
Amendment negatived: Yeas, 20; nays, 44.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Furthermore, I am told that there is a citation with regard to the matter. There is no reason why we should be surprised. What is the number of the citation? I do not have it before me at the moment. I think the point is now being looked into by the Clerk.
Ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am trying to recall situations where resolutions were reported with amendments. I remember that when I was chairman of committees there were occasions when amendments were made in the committee but they were not reported. There is no use in reporting a resolution with amendments because the resolution is in fact an order for leave to introduce a bill. The resolution is studied in committee of the whole and what is done in committee of the whole is to examine how the order for leave to introduce the bill is going to be drafted. Resolutions are reported from the committee of the whole as being the product of the committee of the whole. It is not the same as in the case of a bill which is sent to committee of the whole for examination with a view to possibly being amended. A resolution is not sent there for that purpose; it is sent there to determine if it contains sufficient cause to grant leave to introduce a bill based on the resolution.
It may be that by this time some specific reference in the book has been found, but in any event I am satisfied that is the situation. In the case of amendments to bills we do ask that the amendments be read the first time and concurred in. In this case we ask that the resolutions in their original form or amended be approved by the house. I think that will cover the point if amendments were made to the resolutions.
Resolutions read the second time and concurred in.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
By this time we have found the citation. It is citation 491 of Beauchesne, third edition. I think once more we will all applaud the efficiency of the Clerk of the House. The citation reads as follows:
If a resolution is amended in the committees of the whole, supply or ways and means, the chairman does not report it "with amendments", because
it had not been discussed in the house, when the Speaker was in the chair, prior to being referred to the committee. The resolution is not considered by the house in the same way as a bill which, under standing order 75, is read twice before committal. The terms of the resolution are submitted for the consideration of the house for the first time when the resolution is reported from committee. As the house up to that moment has not considered the merits of the resolution, the committee's amendments do not change anything that has been done by the house and no matter how much the resolution has been altered by the committee, it is reported with all its alterations, but without the mention of amendments.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: In other words, we call them alterations but not amendments.
